method-overview.title: The recipe in ten steps
method-overview.body:
The renormalised action Sren=S0+δS(1)+ΔSST(1) is obtained by the one-loop case of a construction defined at every loop order. Its ten steps are the following.

  1. Model. Propagators and vertices of the regularised action S0 in d=4−2⁢ϵ dimensions, with sterile partners, ghosts and BRST sources as non-propagating legs, and the vertex of the breaking Δ1 (breaking).
  2. Ghost-number-zero graphs. The one-loop 1PI graphs of the ten classes with total dimension of the legs at most 4.
  3. R-operation. At one loop the forest is empty: each graph G is subtracted by −KT(deg(G))G, its pole after expansion to its superficial degree.
  4. Numerator algebra. The BMHV algebra, traces with γ5, tensor reduction and the evanescent tag η (BMHV algebra).
  5. Pole matching. δS(1) on a basis of local operators, invariant and evanescent (field constants, evanescent part).
  6. Breaking vertices. Δ1 and the tree vertex 𝐛dδS(1).
  7. Insertion graphs. The one-loop graphs of the eight ghost-number-one classes with exactly one Δ1 vertex.
  8. Finite breaking. The poles cancel class by class against 𝐛dδS(1); the projected coefficient of ηϵ gives X1.
  9. Restoring condition. Solve 𝐛ΔSST(1)=−X1 under the normalisation conditions (Slavnov–Taylor operator, normalisation).
  10. Model update. Add δS(1) and ΔSST(1) in their d-dimensional forms as counterterm vertices.

In the report all steps were carried out by hand and with stand-alone codes; the graphs were generated with HepKIT. The automation package of this repository runs the same ten steps from a model specification and reproduces the report's constants, breaking and restoring coefficients. Its graphs are the ones drawn on this site.

method-bmhv.title: The BMHV algebra in one screen
method-bmhv.body:
In d=4−2⁢ϵ dimensions every index, momentum and Dirac matrix is split into a four-dimensional (barred) and a (d−4)-dimensional (hatted) part: gμν=g‾μν+gˆμν, kμ=k‾μ+kˆμ, γμ=γ‾μ+γˆμ, with g‾μνgˆνρ=0, g‾μμ=4 and gˆμμ=−4+d. The matrix γ5=i⁢γ0γ1γ2γ3 and the Levi-Civita symbol εμνρσ are four-dimensional, and

{γ‾μ,γ5}=0

[γˆμ,γ5]=0

so γ5 does not anticommute with the full γμ. With PL=1−γ52 and PR=1+γ52, PRγμPL=γ‾μPL and PLγμPL=γˆμPL. A trace with one γ5 and four Dirac matrices is −4⁢i⁢εμνρσ, and only the barred parts contribute.

The physical projection 𝒫 sets every hatted external momentum, metric and Dirac matrix to zero, after all index contractions; an operator with vanishing projection is evanescent. 𝒫 does not commute with the loop integration: inside a loop kˆμkˆμ gives a trace of the hatted metric.

To separate an evanescent contraction from an ultraviolet pole, the trace of the hatted metric is written gˆμμ=−2⁢η, including kˆ2→−2⁢η⁢k2d under the integral, and η is set to ϵ only at the end; every other factor of d is written 4−2⁢ϵ. After expansion with the Taylor operator to its superficial degree around an auxiliary mass, every one-loop graph takes the form

T(deg(G))G=116π2⁢i⁢(η⁢N1ϵ+N0ϵ)+FM

with polynomials N0, N1 in the external momenta and masses and finite terms FM that depend on the auxiliary mass and are never used. N0 gives the pole, N1 the evanescent-induced finite part. Graphs without Δ1 have four-dimensional fermion numerators and N1=0.

method-st.title: The Slavnov–Taylor operator and the restoring equation
method-st.body:
The Slavnov–Taylor operator 𝒮(F) of a functional F of fields and sources is quadratic: it sums the products of the derivative of F with respect to each source ρaμ, ζa, R‾f, Rf, σ†, σ and the derivative with respect to its field, plus the term of the auxiliary field. Its linearisation at the tree action is 𝐛d in d dimensions and 𝐛 in four, with 𝐛𝐛=0. The identity 𝒮(Γ)=0 for the effective action is the content of BRST invariance; in the regularised theory 𝒮(S0)=Δ1 is not zero.

For the effective action the regularised quantum action principle states that 𝒮(Γ) equals the insertion of 𝒮(Sren) into Γ. On graphs the left side is a sum of products of two 1PI functions glued at a source leg and its field leg without propagator; the right side is the sum of 1PI graphs with exactly one breaking vertex. At one loop the left side is one loop function glued to one tree vertex.

𝐛Y of a local functional Y is a set of tree vertices of ghost number 1, built from the vertices of Y with the ghost ωa of polarisation ua and incoming momentum q: an added gauge leg with polarisation −i⁢qμ⁢ua (the ghost-momentum contraction); each gauge, ghost and matter leg rotated by the ghost with its momentum shifted by q; and each source leg replaced by the amputated leg of its field on a tree vertex of S0 (an equation of motion).

At one loop the restoring condition reads, for every ghost-number-one class of external legs,

V𝐛ΔSST(1)=−X1

The left side is the vertex function of 𝐛ΔSST(1), linear in the unknown coefficients rα; the right side is the finite, projected sum X1 of the graphs with one Δ1 vertex, after their poles have cancelled against 𝐛dδS(1). Matching all classes gives an overdetermined linear system with a unique solution under the normalisation conditions; the Wess–Zumino condition 𝐛X1=0 and the absence of an anomaly are its consistency conditions.

method-beyond.title: Beyond one loop
method-beyond.body:
At order l the same identities hold: δS(l) is minus the pole of the graphs of order l, with all subdivergences subtracted by the forest formula of ℛ‾; the breaking Δ[l] collects Δ1, the variations under 𝐛d of the singular counterterms up to order l and of the finite ones below order l, and the products of source-dependent counterterms; Xl is the finite, projected part of their insertions, and 𝐛ΔS(l)=−Xl is solved over the same basis with the same normalisation conditions.

Three things change at two loops. The singular counterterm can contain non-evanescent non-invariant poles. The evanescent parts of δS(1) and the d-dimensional form of ΔSST(1) enter the two-loop graphs and change X2; they must be kept exactly as at one loop. The source counterterms enter quadratically. Since the hypercharge ghost can then sit on an internal line, the existence condition of (N4) must be checked again.

The finite part of the two-loop breaking is local only after the sum of four classes of graphs. It can be obtained in two bookkeepings. In bookkeeping A the one-loop subgraphs that contain Δ1 are not subtracted, and X2 needs the complete finite parts of all classes. In bookkeeping B (the prescription of Lazopoulos et al.) these subgraphs are subtracted at fixed η with K(η), the pole part with η kept until the last integration, and a purely evanescent remainder of one loop is inserted; then UV-expanded integrals suffice.

Status, as stated in the report: the one-loop extraction is proven; bookkeeping A is exact at every order; bookkeeping B is shown at two loops, checked on a toy two-loop graph and consistent with the published abelian two-loop breaking; its extension beyond two loops is argued but not tested on any graph. No two-loop calculation in the Standard Model was done. The automation package supports one loop only and lists what is missing for two: a two-loop back-end, the subtraction of subdivergences, graphs with counterterm insertions, the source–field products of the breaking and the remainder of bookkeeping B.

gauge-kinetic.title: Gauge kinetic terms
gauge-kinetic.body:
The twelve gauge fields Aμa (eight gluons GμA, three fields WμI and the hypercharge field Bμ) enter the classical action through the Yang–Mills Lagrangian −14⁢FμνaFaμν, with Fμνa=∂μAνa−∂νAμa+𝔣abcAμbAνc and the coupling-weighted structure constants 𝔣abc (gs⁢fACD for SU(3), g⁢εIJK for SU(2), zero for U(1)). All its Lorentz indices are d-dimensional, d=4−2⁢ϵ; the term is BRST invariant in d dimensions and does not contribute to the breaking. Since the auxiliary field ba is kept as a field, the tree-level two-point function is the transverse −(gμν⁢p2−pμ⁢pν)⁢δab; the gauge fixing sits in the ba–Aμb function (gauge fixing).

With a non-anticommuting γ5 the chiral gauge vertex contains only the four-dimensional matrix γ‾μ, so fermions couple only to the four-dimensional components A‾μa and fermion loops have four-dimensional numerators with d-dimensional denominators. The one-loop pole of the gauge two-point function therefore has three tensor structures: the unsplit transverse tensor of the gauge, ghost and Higgs loops, the barred transverse tensor g‾μν⁢p‾2−p‾μ⁢p‾ν of the fermion loops, and the evanescent, non-transverse remainder g‾μν⁢pˆ2 of the fermion loops (bars denote four-dimensional and hats (d−4)-dimensional parts).

The coefficient is fixed by the class AA (Section 4.1.1; 20 graphs of superficial degree 2): each graph G is expanded with the Taylor operator T(2) around an auxiliary mass, and minus its pole, −KT(2)G, is its contribution to the counterterm vertex. With A0=ZAA the field-renormalisation constant is

δZA(r)=116π21ϵ⁢(5⁢Cad(r)3−2⁢S(r)3−SH(r)3)

where Cad(r) is the adjoint Casimir (3⁢gs2, 2⁢g2, 0), S(r) the fermion-loop sum of Tr(𝒯a𝒯b) (2⁢gs2, 2⁢g2, 103g′2) and SH(r) the Higgs value (0, 12g2, 12g′2); in units of 116π21ϵ this is 113gs2, 116g2 and −4318g′2. The fermion-loop parts not carried by the continued invariant form the evanescent counterterms. Since the gauge fixing is not renormalised, the invariant two-point counterterm is transverse; the finite restoring counterterm adds a longitudinal term (finite gauge counterterms).

gauge-self.title: Cubic and quartic gauge self-interactions
gauge-self.body:
The cubic and quartic terms of −14⁢FμνaFaμν couple the gluons among themselves and the WμI fields among themselves through the coupling-weighted structure constants 𝔣abc (gs⁢fACD and g⁢εIJK); the abelian field Bμ has no self-coupling. The three-gauge Feynman rule is 𝔣abc⁢(gρμ⁢(−p1+p3)ν+gμν⁢(p1−p2)ρ+gνρ⁢(p2−p3)μ) with all momenta incoming, and the four-gauge rule is −i times the usual sum of products 𝔣abx⁢𝔣cex with differences of metrics. All metrics and momenta are d-dimensional, d=4−2⁢ϵ.

As for the two-point function, the fermion loops couple only to the four-dimensional components A‾μa and give the barred form of the tree vertex, while gauge, ghost and Higgs loops give its d-dimensional form. The poles of the classes AAA (Section 4.1.2; 54 graphs, superficial degree 1) and AAAA (Section 4.1.3; 237 graphs, degree 0) are combinations of these two structures, with the fermion-loop coefficient 23⁢S(r) in both, S(r) being the sum of Tr(𝒯a𝒯b) over the fermion multiplets. The difference between barred and d-dimensional structures is the evanescent operator E˜F(r), whose coefficient is the same in the two-, three- and four-point functions (evanescent counterterms). Mixed and abelian combinations have no pole.

In bare quantities the cubic term carries ZA32⁢Zcr and the quartic term ZA2⁢Zcr2, with cr the coupling of the factor r. The counterterm factors are

3⁢δZA(r)2+δZcr=116π21ϵ⁢(2⁢Cad(r)3−2⁢S(r)3−SH(r)3)

2⁢δZA(r)+2⁢δZcr=116π21ϵ⁢(−Cad(r)3−2⁢S(r)3−SH(r)3)

with Cad(r) the adjoint Casimir and SH(r) the Higgs trace; in units of 116π21ϵ the cubic factor is 23gs2 and −16g2, the quartic one −73gs2 and −136g2. One field constant and one coupling constant per gauge factor fit the classes AA, AAA, AAAA and the ghost functions together; the report lists these cross-class conditions as a check (Section 4.3.1). The finite restoring counterterm contains cubic and quartic gauge terms as well, some without a tree-level counterpart (finite gauge counterterms).

gauge-fixing.title: Linear gauge fixing and the auxiliary field
gauge-fixing.body:
For each of the twelve gauge fields there is a ghost ωa, an antighost ω‾a and an auxiliary field ba. The gauge-fixing Lagrangian is

12ξ⁢baba+ba∂μAμa+(∂μω‾a)(Dμω)a

a linear covariant gauge. Together with the BRST source terms it is BRST exact: it is the BRST variation 𝐬 of ω‾a(ξ⁢ba2+∂μAμa) plus source terms, with 𝐬ω‾a=ba and 𝐬ba=0, and hence BRST invariant in d dimensions. Every calculation is done in the Feynman gauge ξ=1, where eliminating ba gives −12⁢(∂μAμa)2, with the gauge propagator −i⁢gμν⁢δabk2 and a d-dimensional metric.

The gauge fixing is not renormalised. Because it is linear in the quantum fields, the identity δΓδba=ξ⁢ba+∂μAμa holds exactly in the regularised theory and for every counterterm: ba never appears inside a loop, functions with an external ba are tree level, and no such class is computed. In bare quantities ba, ω‾a and the source ρaμ scale with 1ZA and ξ0=ξ⁢ZA, so the gauge-fixing term receives no counterterm and the invariant gauge two-point counterterm is transverse. The companion identity for the antighost is the ghost equation (ghost terms).

The gauge fixing contains no fermion and plays no role in the breaking. Its form matters for the broken phase: it does not depend on the Higgs doublet, so the shift H→Hv+φ leaves it unchanged and the broken-phase action needs no further loop input (broken phase). An Rξ gauge, which removes the gauge–Goldstone mixing, depends on Hv; the report describes the additional input it would need but does not compute it (Section 5.5.3). The dependence on ξ was not computed: all results hold at ξ=1.

ghost.title: Ghost terms and the ghost equation
ghost.body:
The Faddeev–Popov term (∂μω‾a)(Dμω)a, with (Dμω)a=∂μωa+𝔣abcAμbωc, contains the ghost kinetic term (propagator i⁢δabk2) and the ghost–gauge vertex with Feynman rule −𝔣abc⁢p′μ, where p′ is the outgoing momentum of the antighost ω‾a. Ghosts are Grassmann odd and carry ghost number 1; a closed ghost loop carries a factor −1. They couple only to gauge fields, and the ghost ωB of the abelian factor is free.

By the ghost equation δΓδω‾a+∂μδΓδρaμ=0, which holds exactly because it is linear in the quantum fields, the effective action Γ depends on the antighost and on the source ρaμ of 𝐬Aμa only through ρ˜aμ=ρaμ+∂μω‾a. Green's functions with an external antighost therefore follow from those with an external ρaμ. The ghost counterterms are fixed by the functions ρω, ρAω and ζωω of the class of ghost and BRST-source functions (Section 4.1.10; 20 graphs), where ζa is the source of 𝐬ωa.

With ω0=Zωω the ghost constant is δZω(r)=116π21ϵ⁢(8⁢Cad(r)3−2⁢S(r)3−SH(r)3) (203gs2 and 236g2 in units of 116π21ϵ), with Cad(r) the adjoint Casimir, S(r) the fermion trace and SH(r) the Higgs trace. The ghost kinetic counterterm has the coefficient δZω(r)−δZA(r)2=116π21ϵ⁢Cad(r)2, and the ghost–gauge vertex and all non-linear source terms share δZω(r)2+δZcr=−116π21ϵ⁢Cad(r)2, i.e. −32gs2 and −g2. In the abelian factor every ghost counterterm vanishes.

Ghost loops are d-dimensional and covariant and give no evanescent pole. The ghost does enter the breaking Δ1, where it multiplies the evanescent fermion kinetic term, and in the classes with external fermions the ghost of Δ1 can be an internal line that ends on a ghost–gauge vertex. The finite restoring counterterm has no ghost kinetic and no ghost–gauge term; its only ghost-dependent term is the fermion source term.

fermion-kinetic.title: Fermion kinetic terms and sterile partners
fermion-kinetic.body:
Each chiral multiplet f (Q, U, D, L, E) has a physical field ψf of chirality cf (left-handed for Q and L, right-handed for U, D and E) and a sterile partner χf of the opposite chirality. The partner has the colour and SU(2) indices of ψf and transforms like it under global transformations, but it is a singlet under all gauge groups. The pair forms one Dirac field Ψf=ψf+χf, ψf=PcfΨf, whose kinetic term Ψ‾fi/∂Ψf is the complete d-dimensional Dirac operator, while the gauge interaction Ψ‾fγ‾μ𝒯faPcfΨfAμa contains only the four-dimensional γ‾μ and the physical chirality.

The sterile partners are needed for the propagator: i⁢/kk2 is the inverse of the complete d-dimensional kinetic operator, which is what makes a gauge vertex contracted with the ghost momentum cancel the adjacent propagators. In chiral components the kinetic term contains, besides iψ‾fγ‾μDμψf and the free term of χf, the evanescent terms iψ‾fγˆμ∂μχf+iχ‾fγˆμ∂μψf. They are not gauge invariant; they are the only place where the regularisation breaks the gauge symmetry, and their BRST variation is the breaking Δ1. Between two physical vertices the propagator is Pcfi⁢/kk2Pc‾f=i⁢/k‾k2Pc‾f: in a graph without Δ1 the Dirac algebra is four-dimensional and the regularisation acts only through the integrals.

The class Ψ‾Ψ (Section 4.1.4; 16 graphs, superficial degree 1) has the pole 116π21ϵ⁢(Cf+𝒴f)⁢/p‾Pcf and no evanescent part. Only the physical component is renormalised, ψf0=Zfψf, with

δZf=−116π21ϵ⁢(Cf+𝒴f)

where Cf=∑a𝒯fa𝒯fa is the Casimir of the multiplet and 𝒴f its Yukawa part (12(yu2+yd2), yu2, yd2, 12ye2, ye2 on Q, U, D, L, E); for Q, δZQ=−116π21ϵ⁢(yu2+yd22+4⁢gs23+3⁢g24+g′236). The sterile partners and the evanescent kinetic terms are not renormalised. The normalisation condition (N1) excludes a finite fermion kinetic counterterm (normalisation).

fermion-gauge.title: Fermion–gauge vertices
fermion-gauge.body:
The fermions couple to the gauge fields through Ψ‾fγ‾μ𝒯faPcfΨfAμa, with the coupling-weighted generators 𝒯fa (gs⁢TA, 12g⁢τI, g′⁢Yf) and the projector Pcf on the physical chirality. The Feynman rule is i⁢γ‾μPcf𝒯fa. A chiral coupling can be written consistently only with the four-dimensional γ‾μ, which anticommutes with γ5 while γˆμ commutes with it; the fermions therefore see only the four-dimensional gauge field A‾μa. This four-dimensional vertex next to a d-dimensional kinetic term is the origin of every finite breaking of the Slavnov–Taylor identity.

Contracting the vertex with the incoming ghost momentum q gives two inverse propagators, which cancel the adjacent propagators as in a theory with an anticommuting γ5, plus the vertex of the tree-level breaking Δ1 (Section 2.2.1). In a loop the inverse propagators cancel pairwise along the cycle after shifts of the loop momentum; what remains is the graph with the gauge vertex replaced by Δ1.

The class Ψ‾ΨA (Section 4.1.5; 46 graphs, superficial degree 0) covers the ten pairs of a multiplet f and a gauge factor r acting on it. Its pole has no evanescent part and is proportional to the tree vertex, with the counterterm factor

δZf+δZA(r)2+δZcr=−116π21ϵ⁢(Cf+Cad(r)+𝒴f)

where Cf is the Casimir of the multiplet, Cad(r) the adjoint Casimir of the factor and 𝒴f the Yukawa part of the fermion constant. The report checks that the coefficients of the vertex and of the kinetic monomial differ by −Cad(r) for all ten pairs (Section 4.3.1). The finite restoring counterterm adds a four-dimensional vertex with the coefficient −12⁢νfr−Cf (times 116π2), where νfr are Yukawa numbers (finite fermion counterterms).

yukawa.title: Yukawa couplings
yukawa.body:
With one fermion family the Yukawa couplings yu, yd, ye are real numbers without flavour mixing:

−yu⁢Q‾H˜PRU−yd⁢Q‾HPRD−ye⁢L‾HPRE+h.c.

with H˜i=εijHj*. Only physical components enter, because Q‾PR is the conjugate of the left-handed quark doublet and PRU is the right-handed up quark; the sterile partners never couple to the Higgs doublet. The Yukawa terms are BRST invariant in d dimensions and do not contribute to the breaking Δ1.

The class Ψ‾ΨH (Section 4.1.9; 32 graphs, superficial degree 0) has a pole proportional to the tree vertex. With yk0=μϵ⁢(yk+δyk) the vertex counterterm is the tree rule times 12(δZH+δZf+δZf′)+δykyk, where f and f′ are the two multiplets of the vertex. For the up-type coupling

δyuyu=116π21ϵ⁢(−4⁢gs2−9⁢g28−17⁢g′224+9⁢yu24+3⁢yd24+ye22)

which gives the beta function βyu=116π2⁢yu⁢(−8⁢gs2−9⁢g24−17⁢g′212+9⁢yu22+3⁢yd22+ye2), in agreement with the known one-family value.

The finite restoring counterterm contains no Yukawa vertex: the real and imaginary Yukawa monomials are invariant directions, and the normalisation condition (N1) sets their finite coefficients to zero (normalisation). The Yukawa couplings still enter the finite counterterms of other vertices through fermion loops (the numbers νfr of the fermion–gauge vertices and Y˜ of the scalar–gauge vertices). In the class ωΨ‾ΨH (Section 4.2.7; 122 graphs) the finite breaking is non-zero only for the SU(2) ghost and is reproduced by the finite fermion source terms; it has no component along the hypercharge ghost ωB, which is one of the existence conditions of the normalisation (N4).

higgs-kinetic.title: Higgs kinetic term and scalar–gauge vertices
higgs-kinetic.body:
The Higgs doublet H (hypercharge 1/2, colour singlet) has the d-dimensional kinetic term (DμH)†DμH with the covariant derivative Dμ=−i⁢𝒯HaAμa+∂μ, where 𝒯Ha are the coupling-weighted generators on the doublet (12g⁢τI and 12g′). Its Feynman rules are the propagator i⁢δij−m2+k2 and the vertices i⁢(p+p′)μ⁢𝒯Ha for H†HA and i⁢gμν⁢{𝒯Ha,𝒯Hb} for H†HAA. The term contains no fermion and is BRST invariant in d dimensions.

The scalar functions receive two kinds of loops. Bosonic loops are d-dimensional and covariant. The Yukawa fermion loops have four-dimensional numerators and couple only to A‾μa, so they give barred structures. The pole of the Higgs two-point function (Section 4.1.6; 8 graphs) is 116π21ϵ⁢(6⁢λ⁢m2+Y˜⁢(23⁢pˆ2+p‾2)−(m2+2⁢p2)⁢CH), with Y˜=3⁢yu2+3⁢yd2+ye2 and CH=3⁢g24+g′24. The field constant, defined by H0=ZHH, is

δZH=116π21ϵ⁢(−Y˜+2⁢CH)

and multiplies the continued d-dimensional invariant; the barred and hatted remainders of the fermion loops are the evanescent counterterms E˜H and EH (evanescent counterterms).

The functions H†HA and H†HAA (Section 4.1.7; 146 graphs) give the vertex factors δZH+δZcr+12δZA(r), equal to 116π21ϵ⁢(−Y˜+2⁢CH−Cad(r)) for one gauge leg and 116π21ϵ⁢(−Y˜+2⁢CH−Cad(r)−Cad(s)) for two, with Cad(r) the adjoint Casimir of the factor of each gauge leg; the functions with an external gluon have no pole. The Yukawa loops also break the Slavnov–Taylor identity at finite level; the restoring terms have purely Yukawa coefficients (finite scalar counterterms).

higgs-potential.title: Scalar potential: mass and quartic terms
higgs-potential.body:
The potential is −λ⁢(H†H)2−m2⁢H†H. The unbroken phase is the expansion around H=0; m2 is a real parameter of either sign, the Higgs propagator is i−m2+k2 and the quartic Feynman rule is −2⁢λ⁢i⁢(δij⁢δkl+δil⁢δkj). The potential contains no fermion, is BRST invariant in d dimensions and plays no role in the breaking.

The mass counterterm follows from the Higgs two-point function (Section 4.1.6; 8 graphs, superficial degree 2) and the quartic one from the four-point function (Section 4.1.8; 63 graphs, degree 0). With m02=m2+δm2 and λ0=μ2⁢ϵ⁢(λ+δλ),

δm2=116π21ϵ⁢m2⁢(6⁢λ+Y˜−3⁢CH)

δλ=116π21ϵ⁢(2⁢λ⁢Y˜−6⁢λ⁢CH−Y4+3⁢G416+12⁢λ2)

where CH=3⁢g24+g′24, Y˜=3⁢yu2+3⁢yd2+ye2, Y4=3⁢yu4+3⁢yd4+ye4 and G4=2⁢g2⁢g′2+3⁢g4+g′4. They give βλ=116π2⁢(4⁢λ⁢Y˜−3⁢λ⁢(3⁢g2+g′2)−2⁢Y4+3⁢G48+24⁢λ2), the known one-family value.

There is no finite counterterm in this sector. The mass and quartic monomials are invariant directions, and the normalisation condition (N1) sets their finite coefficients to zero (normalisation). The finite breaking does not depend on m2: in a one-loop graph with Δ1, Higgs propagators occur only in classes with external fermions, whose local part has dimensionless coefficients. Hence there is no finite gauge-boson mass term at H=0, and the breaking vanishes in the class ωH†HH†H. The potential is renormalised by the MS-bar poles alone, in the broken phase as well (masses).

brst-sources.title: BRST source terms
brst-sources.body:
The BRST operator 𝐬 acts as 𝐬Aμa=(Dμω)a, 𝐬ωa=−𝔣abcωbωc2, 𝐬Ψf=i⁢ωa𝒯faPcfΨf and 𝐬H=i⁢ωa𝒯HaH; the sterile partners do not transform. The non-linear variations are coupled to external sources that never propagate and have the statistics opposite to their field:

σ†𝐬H+ζa𝐬ωa+(𝐬H†)σ+ρaμ𝐬Aμa+∑f(R‾f𝐬Ψf−(𝐬Ψ‾f)Rf)

The sources make the Slavnov–Taylor operator possible: for a functional F of fields and sources, 𝒮(F) is the integral of a sum of products of a derivative with respect to a source and one with respect to its field, for example δFδρaμδFδAμa, plus baδFδω‾a. For the tree action the source derivative of S0 is the BRST variation of the field, so 𝒮(S0)=𝐬S0=Δ1. The linearised operator 𝐛d acts as 𝐬 on the fields and replaces each source by plus or minus the equation of motion of its field. A counterterm that depends on sources changes the BRST transformations themselves.

The source functions ρω, ρAω, ζωω, R‾ωΨ, σ†ωH and their conjugates form one class (Section 4.1.10; 20 graphs). With the sources scaled inversely to their fields, all non-linear source terms share one coefficient, −116π21ϵ⁢12Cad(r) (−32gs2 and −g2 in units of 116π21ϵ; zero for the hypercharge), and the linear term of ρaμ has 116π21ϵ⁢12Cad(r), with Cad(r) the adjoint Casimir. In d dimensions 𝐛d of the fermion source counterterm contains the breaking Δ1(fr) of the multiplet f and the factor r; this is the term that cancels the evanescent pole of the ωΨ‾Ψ graphs with an internal ghost (Section 4.3.2). Of all source terms only the fermion ones receive a finite counterterm.

breaking.title: The tree-level breaking Δ₁
breaking.body:
Every term of the regularised action S0 except the evanescent fermion kinetic terms is BRST invariant in d dimensions. Applying 𝐬 to the fermion Lagrangian, the variation of the gauge vertex cancels the four-dimensional part of the variation of the kinetic term, and what remains is

Δ1=∑f∫ddx(ωaΨ‾f𝒯faγˆμPc‾f∂μΨf+ωa(∂μΨ‾f)γˆμPcf𝒯faΨf)

an integrated local operator of ghost number 1 and dimension 5 coupling a ghost, a physical fermion and its sterile partner through the evanescent matrix γˆμ; its physical projection vanishes, 𝒫Δ1=0. Its sign agrees with Bělusca-Maïto et al. (arXiv:2004.14398) and with Lazopoulos et al. (arXiv:2610.38618) and is opposite to eq. (1.18) of the BMHV starter pack read with the ghost as the leftmost factor. Δ1 is not part of the action; it is listed for its Feynman rule. With Ψf entering with momentum p, Ψ‾f leaving with p′ and the ghost ωa carrying −p+p′, the rule is

i⁢VΔ1=𝒯fa(/pˆPc‾f−/p′ˆPcf)

When the external ghost sits on Δ1, both fermion legs are internal, one is the sterile component, and vertex and sterile propagator combine into the scalar insertion i⁢𝒯aqˆ2q2 on a physical fermion line (Eq. (6)). If its ghost is internal (classes with external fermions), Δ1 sits at an external fermion leg (Section 4.2).

Δ1 is what determines the finite counterterm. By the regularised quantum action principle, 𝒮(Γ) equals the insertion of 𝒮(Sren) into the effective action. At one loop this insertion consists of the one-loop graphs with exactly one Δ1 vertex plus the tree vertex 𝐛dδS(1): their poles cancel class by class, and their finite part, projected on four dimensions, is the breaking X1, iX1=∑G𝒫116π2⁢i⁢N1, with N1 the coefficient of ηϵ in the expanded graph G and 𝒫 the projection on four-dimensional external momenta and indices (Slavnov–Taylor operator). X1 is local and independent of the auxiliary mass because Δ1 is evanescent: only graphs of non-negative superficial degree with an internal sterile line next to Δ1 contribute, and no reading point enters.

ct-fields.title: Field renormalisation constants
ct-fields.body:
The singular counterterm δS(1) is fixed graph by graph. Every one-loop 1PI graph G of a ghost-number-zero class is expanded with the Taylor operator T(deg(G)) to its superficial degree deg(G) around an auxiliary mass; its MS-bar pole part is KT(deg(G))G=116π21ϵ⁢i⁢N0 (d=4−2⁢ϵ), and minus the sum over the graphs with given external legs is the Feynman rule of the counterterm vertex. These graphs have no evanescent finite part, N1=0, and evanescent and non-invariant pole structures are kept.

In four dimensions the poles lie in the 25-dimensional kernel of the linearised Slavnov–Taylor operator 𝐛 on the 97 monomials Qα of the restoring basis: 25 coefficients fix the invariant directions and the other 72 are predictions, all of which hold. The invariant part of δS(1) is therefore the first-order term of S0 written in bare quantities, A0=ZAA, ω0=Zωω, ψf0=Zfψf, H0=ZHH, with every source scaled by the inverse factor of its field, one constant per gauge factor and Zx=1+δZx. The sterile partners and the gauge fixing are not renormalised. Each constant δZx includes the factor 116π21ϵ.

In the Feynman gauge, in units of 116π21ϵ: δZA(r) is 113gs2, 116g2, −4318g′2 for the gluon, W and B fields; δZω(r) is 203gs2 and 236g2; δZf=−(Cf+𝒴f) for the five fermion multiplets, with Cf the Casimir and 𝒴f the Yukawa part; and δZH=−Y˜+3⁢g22+g′22 with Y˜ the Yukawa sum 3⁢yu2+3⁢yd2+ye2. They agree with the standard Feynman-gauge values, and the automation reproduces all twenty constants of fields and parameters exactly.

In d dimensions the invariant directions are continued with unsplit d-dimensional indices, fields and derivatives in the bosonic monomials and with the barred vertex ψ‾fγ‾μ𝒜μψf in the fermion monomials. The graphs without a closed fermion loop give exactly these combinations. The closed fermion loops give barred invariants, whose difference from the continued ones is part of the evanescent counterterm.

ct-couplings.title: Coupling and mass counterterms, beta functions
ct-couplings.body:
The parameters are renormalised multiplicatively in MS-bar: cr0=μϵZcrcr for the gauge couplings cr (gs, g, g′), yk0=μϵ⁢(yk+δyk), λ0=μ2⁢ϵ⁢(λ+δλ) and m02=m2+δm2; every counterterm includes 116π21ϵ. For the gauge couplings

δZcr=116π21ϵ⁢(−11⁢Cad(r)6+S(r)3+SH(r)6)

with the adjoint Casimir Cad(r) (3⁢gs2, 2⁢g2, 0), the fermion trace S(r) (2⁢gs2, 2⁢g2, 103g′2) and the Higgs trace SH(r); this is −296gs2, −3512g2 and 4336g′2 in units of 116π21ϵ. For the hypercharge, Zg′ZB=1, with ZB the field constant of Bμ. The Yukawa, quartic and mass constants are given in the cards on Yukawa couplings and the scalar potential.

At one loop the beta function βx of a coupling x is 2⁢x times the coefficient of 116π21ϵ in δxx (with δcr=crδZcr for the gauge couplings), which gives βgs=−29⁢116π2⁢gs33, βg=−35⁢116π2⁢g36 and βg′=43⁢116π2⁢g′318, and the Yukawa and quartic beta functions; all agree with the known one-loop values of the Standard Model with one family (Machacek and Vaughn), and the automation reproduces the eight beta functions.

The non-anticommuting γ5 enters through the d-dimensional form of these counterterms. In four dimensions the coupling direction 𝒪g(r), equal to cr times the derivative of S0 with respect to cr, is invariant under 𝐛. In d dimensions it is not: since Δ1 is linear in the generators of each factor, 𝐛d𝒪g(r)=Δ1(r), the part of the breaking with the ghosts of the factor r. The coupling and ghost counterterms thereby contribute −116π21ϵ⁢12Cad(r)⁢Δ1(r) to 𝐛dδS(1), which predicts the evanescent pole of the ωΨ‾Ψ functions; the class result agrees (Section 4.3.2).

ct-evanescent.title: Evanescent singular counterterms
ct-evanescent.body:
Fermion loops couple only to the four-dimensional gauge field A‾μa and give barred tensors, while bosonic loops give d-dimensional covariant ones. Hatted external momenta, the (d−4)-dimensional parts, enter only through kˆ⋅pˆ in the denominators and need a superficial degree of at least 2: they occur only in the two-point functions AA and H†H. The one-loop poles therefore contain four evanescent operators, which vanish when all hatted quantities are set to zero:

EA(r)=∫ddx(A‾μa∂ˆ2A‾aμ)2

EH=∫ddx((∂ˆμH)†∂ˆμH)

and E˜F(r), E˜H, the differences between the barred invariants −14⁢F‾μνaF‾aμν, (D‾μH)†D‾μH and their d-dimensional counterparts. With S(r) the fermion trace of the factor r and Y˜=3⁢yu2+3⁢yd2+ye2, the evanescent part of δS(1) is

−116π21ϵ⁢(Y˜⁢(23⁢EH+E˜H)+∑r(EA(r)3+2⁢E˜F(r)3)⁢S(r))

In the Standard Model the coefficients of EA(r) are −116π21ϵ times 23gs2, 23g2, 109g′2, that of EH is −116π21ϵ⁢23Y˜, those of E˜F(r) are −116π21ϵ times 43gs2, 43g2, 209g′2, and that of E˜H is −116π21ϵ⁢Y˜. The coefficient of E˜F(r) is the same in the two-, three- and four-point functions. No fermion bilinear carries an evanescent pole.

E˜F(r) and E˜H are invariant under 𝐛d; EA(r) and EH are the two non-invariant singular counterterms of one loop. Their variations, 𝐛dEA(r)=NˆAA(r)+NˆA(r) and 𝐛dEH=NˆH, are evanescent operators of ghost number 1, and they predict the evanescent poles of the classes ωA, ωAA and ωH†H; the class results agree (Section 4.3.2). These operators do not affect four-dimensional one-loop quantities, but they must be kept in their d-dimensional form: inserted into a loop, the hatted derivatives of EA(r) become the hatted loop momentum, −kˆ2, and give ηϵ2, hence a pole and a finite part at two loops.

st-gauge.title: Finite restoring counterterms of the gauge sector
st-gauge.body:
The finite counterterm is ΔSST(1)=116π2⁢∑αrα⁢Qα, with four-dimensional monomials Qα and rational coefficients rα. Its gauge part is 116π2 times the expression below, with the matrix-valued field 𝒜μ=𝒯faAμa in the representation of each fermion multiplet f and all objects four-dimensional,

∫d4x(∑fTr((13𝒜μ𝒜μ𝒜ν𝒜ν−14𝒜μ𝒜ν𝒜μ𝒜ν+16(∂μ𝒜μ)∂ν𝒜ν−i3(∂μ𝒜ν)[𝒜μ,𝒜ν])))

a sum of traces over the fermion multiplets. In the gauge classes the ghost of the breaking vertex is external and the loop is a closed fermion loop, the only kind of loop that sees the breaking.

The coefficients follow from 𝐛ΔSST(1)=−X1, class by class. In the class ωA (Section 4.2.1; 10 graphs with one breaking vertex) the finite breaking is −116π2⁢13⁢N3(r)⁢S(r), with N3(r)=∫d4x(ωa∂2∂μAaμ) and S(r) the sum of Tr(𝒯a𝒯b) over the multiplets (2⁢gs2, 2⁢g2, 103g′2). The longitudinal monomial QL(r)=−12∫d4x((∂μAaμ)2) has 𝐛QL(r)=−N3(r), so rQL(r)=−S(r)3: −23gs2, −23g2, −109g′2. The mass monomial gets no coefficient: there is no finite gauge-boson mass term. The class ωAA (Section 4.2.2; 40 graphs) fixes the cubic coefficient rQ3⁢f(r)=−S(r)3 and checks the longitudinal one; the classes ωAAA and ωAAAA (Section 4.2.3; 1320 graphs) fix the thirteen quartic coefficients (for example 11/72, −1/4 and 5/12 for the three gluon monomials and 95/648 for g′4⁢(BμBμ)2), and the five-point breaking vanishes identically.

The normalisation (N2) excludes the transverse monomial QT(r), which is invariant (normalisation). Several monomials have no tree-level counterpart, for instance the quartic hypercharge term and a gluon–gluon–gluon–B term with the symmetric tensor dACD. The report checks the result with complete MS-bar finite parts: the fermion loops of the renormalised self-energy give pμΓμν=−13116π2S(r)p2pν (times δab) and the longitudinal term adds the opposite, so the self-energy is transverse (Section 4.3.7).

st-fermion.title: Finite restoring counterterms of the fermion–gauge vertices
st-fermion.body:
The fermion part of the finite counterterm is a four-dimensional gauge vertex of the physical components,

−116π2⁢∫d4x(∑fψ‾fγμ(Cf⁢𝒜μ+∑r𝒜μ(r)⁢νfr2)ψf)

where Cf is the Casimir of the multiplet f, 𝒜μ(r) the matrix-valued gauge field of the factor r, and νfr are Yukawa numbers: yu2+yd2, 0 and 4⁢yu2−2⁢yd2 for Q with G, W, B; 2⁢yu2 and 12yu2 for U; 2⁢yd2 and −yd2 for D; 0 and 2⁢ye2 for L; ye2 for E. The Feynman rule is −116π2⁢i⁢(12⁢νfr+Cf)⁢γ‾μ𝒯faPcf. Since the Yukawa parts are not proportional to the charges, they cannot be absorbed into a renormalisation of the gauge couplings.

The coefficient is fixed in the class ωΨ‾Ψ (Section 4.2.4; 42 graphs). Its graphs are of two kinds: the external ghost sits on Δ1 and both fermion legs of the vertex are internal, or the ghost of Δ1 is internal and ends on a ghost–gauge vertex that carries the external ghost. The finite breaking is 116π2⁢∑frNFfr⁢xfr, with NFfr=∫d4x(ψ‾fγμ(∂μ𝛚(r))ψf) and xfr=−νfr2−(Cf−Cad(r)4), Cad(r) being the adjoint Casimir. The vertex monomial gives −NFfr under 𝐛 and the fermion source monomial gives NFfr, so rQRfr−rQVfr=−xfr. With the source coefficient −14Cad(r) fixed elsewhere (source terms), rQVfr=−Cf−νfr2: the term 14Cad(r) cancels. The class ωΨ‾ΨA (Section 4.2.5; 220 graphs) confirms the source coefficient.

The normalisation (N1) excludes a finite fermion kinetic term, which would shift rQVfr; the representatives in the literature contain one and differ by invariant terms. The report checks the restored Ward identity of the legs ghost, Ψ‾f, Ψf with complete MS-bar finite parts at off-shell points: without the finite counterterm the violation is −116π2⁢i⁢(12⁢νfr+Cf−14Cad(r))⁢/q‾𝒯faPcf, and the vertex and source terms cancel it to a relative precision of 10−13 (Section 4.3.7).

st-source.title: Finite counterterms of the source terms
st-source.body:
The only term of the finite counterterm that contains a ghost is a finite part of the fermion source terms,

−116π2⁢14⁢∫d4x(∑f(−i⁢ψ‾f𝛚CRf+i⁢R‾f𝛚Cψf))

with 𝛚C=∑rCad(r)⁢𝛚(r), the sum over the non-abelian factors of the adjoint Casimir (3⁢gs2, 2⁢g2) times the matrix-valued ghost 𝛚(r)=𝒯faωa of the factor. In the basis this is rQRfr=−Cad(r)4, i.e. −34gs2 for gluon ghosts and −12g2 for W ghosts; the hypercharge coefficient is zero by the normalisation (N4). The Feynman rules are 116π2⁢14Cad(r)⁢𝒯faPcf for the legs R‾fωaΨf and 116π2⁢14Cad(r)⁢Pc‾f𝒯fa for ωaΨ‾fRf. A source term changes the BRST transformation of the field it multiplies: this counterterm is a finite renormalisation of 𝐬ψf.

The coefficient is fixed by the class ωωR‾Ψ and its conjugate (Section 4.2.8; 54 graphs). Its pole vanishes, N0=0 (Eq. (449)), consistent with 𝐛dδS(1)=0 in this class, where QRfr and Qζ have the same singular coefficient −12Cad(r). Its finite breaking is 116π2⁢14Cad(r) times R‾f𝛚(r)𝛚(r)ψf plus the conjugate structure. The five source classes ωωρ˜, ωωρ˜A, ωωωζ, ωωσ†H and ωωH†σ have no one-loop graph with Δ1, so the breaking vanishes there (Section 4.2; Section 3.8.9); this sets the finite coefficients of the ρaμ, ζa and σ terms to zero, and then rQRfr=−Cad(r)4. The classes ωΨ‾ΨA and ωΨ‾ΨH confirm the value independently.

In d dimensions 𝐛d of the source monomial contains the breaking Δ1(fr), so ℰ𝐛dΔSST(1)=−116π2⁢∑rCad(r)⁢Δ1(r)4, where ℰ is the evanescent part. This has no effect at one loop. At two loops it enters as a vertex of ghost number 1, and the source counterterms enter quadratically through the source–field part of the Slavnov–Taylor operator (beyond one loop).

st-scalar.title: Finite restoring counterterms with scalars
st-scalar.body:
The scalar part of the finite counterterm is, with Y˜=3⁢yu2+3⁢yd2+ye2 and the matrix-valued gauge fields 𝒜(W), 𝒜(B) on the doublet,

116π2⁢∫d4x(Y˜⁢i⁢(−H†𝒜μ∂μH+(∂μH)†𝒜μH)3−Y˜⁢H†𝒜μ(W)𝒜μ(W)H−(yu2+2⁢yd2)⁢H†{𝒜μ(W),𝒜μ(B)}H−(13⁢yu23+7⁢yd23+3⁢ye2)⁢H†𝒜μ(B)𝒜μ(B)H−gs2⁢(yu2+yd2)⁢H†HGμAGAμ2)

with 𝒜=𝒜(W)+𝒜(B) in the first term. Every coefficient is a Yukawa combination: the scalar sector is BRST invariant in d dimensions, and the scalars feel the breaking only through Yukawa fermion loops. There is no finite counterterm for the Higgs kinetic term, the potential or the Yukawa vertices, and none with the Higgs source σ.

The coefficients come from the classes ωH†H, ωH†HA, ωH†HAA and ωH†HH†H (Section 4.2.6; 525 graphs). In ωH†H the breaking is −116π2⁢13Y˜⁢(NS(W)+NS(B)), and the current monomials QJ(r) (the first term above for one factor) give 𝐛QJ(r)=NS(r), hence rQJ(r)=Y˜3 for both factors. In ωH†HA five structures fix the four two-gauge coefficients, with one consistency condition; the breaking of the last two classes vanishes, as does 𝐛ΔSST(1) there. The pole of ωH†H is the evanescent 116π21ϵ⁢23Y˜⁢NˆH, cancelled by the variation of the evanescent counterterm EH.

The report checks the abelian Ward identity of the legs ωB, H†, H with exact bubble and triangle finite parts: the fermion graphs violate it by −116π2⁢16g′⁢Y˜⁢(p12−p22), which the term rQJ(B)⁢QJ(B) cancels to working precision (Section 4.3.7). In the broken phase these terms produce the finite gauge-boson mass terms and the change of the gauge–Goldstone mixing (broken phase).

normalisation.title: Freedom of the finite counterterm and the normalisation conditions
normalisation.body:
The restoring condition 𝐛ΔSST(1)=−X1 fixes ΔSST(1) only up to the kernel of 𝐛, the linearised Slavnov–Taylor operator in four dimensions. On the 97 monomials Qα (four-dimensional, Lorentz and rigidly invariant, hermitian, ghost number 0, dimension at most 4) the image of 𝐛 has dimension 72 and the kernel dimension 25. The 25 invariant directions are the 20 renormalisations of fields and parameters, the three imaginary Yukawa couplings and two charge deformations of the hypercharge (baryon and lepton number). A finite counterterm along them is a finite, invariant renormalisation; it does not restore anything.

The report removes these directions by four conditions on the monomials allowed in ΔSST(1):

  1. (N1) no monomial that survives when all gauge fields, ghosts and sources vanish: the fermion and Higgs kinetic terms, the mass and quartic terms and the six Yukawa monomials (14 monomials);
  2. (N2) no transverse gauge two-point monomial QT(r) (3);
  3. (N3) no source monomial ∫d4x(ρ˜aμ∂μωa) and no ∫d4x(𝔣abcρ˜aμAμbωc) (5);
  4. (N4) no monomial that contains the hypercharge ghost ωB (11).

On the remaining 64 monomials 𝐛 has rank 64, so the solution is unique. It exists only if X1 satisfies eight linear conditions, and all eight hold: five say that X1 vanishes in the source classes, which have no one-loop graph with Δ1; three say that X1 has no component along g′⁢yk⁢i⁢∫d4x(ωB(Ok−Ok†)), with Ok the Yukawa monomials. The latter hold because at one loop the hypercharge ghost has no vertex with two internal lines. Beyond one loop it can sit on an internal line; if the condition fails, (N4) is replaced by (N4′), which keeps the hypercharge source monomials of the right-handed multiplets U, D, E.

With these conditions the finite counterterm contains no fermion kinetic, Yukawa, potential or transverse gauge term: everything invariant is MS-bar. The representatives of Bělusca-Maïto et al. and of Lazopoulos et al. differ from it by invariant terms (Section 4.3.6).

anomaly.title: The would-be gauge anomaly
anomaly.body:
Each fermion multiplet contributes a parity-odd part to the finite breaking X1, with the four-dimensional Levi-Civita symbol εμνρσ from the trace of γ5 with four Dirac matrices. Summed over the multiplets it is proportional to the totally symmetric traces

Dabc=∑lhTr(𝒯fa{𝒯fb,𝒯fc})−∑rhTr(𝒯fa{𝒯fb,𝒯fc})

where lh runs over the left-handed multiplets Q, L and rh over the right-handed U, D, E:

Xanom=116π2⁢(−∫d4x(Dabcεμνρσωa(∂μAνb)∂ρAσc)3+∫d4x(Daed𝔣bceεμνρσ(∂μωa)AνbAρcAσd)12)

It comes from the classes ωAA and ωAAA (Section 4.2.2). Per Weyl multiplet the first term is 116π2⁢23 times εμνρσTr(𝛚(∂μ𝒜ν)∂ρ𝒜σ) up to its sign, the consistent anomaly.

It satisfies the consistency condition 𝐛Xanom=0 multiplet by multiplet, but it does not lie in the image of 𝐛: the only parity-odd monomials of the restoring basis can remove part of it, and what remains lies outside unless the four independent anomaly coefficients vanish. An anomaly cannot be removed by a local counterterm, and the solution of 𝐛ΔSST(1)=−X1 exists only if they vanish.

With the hypercharges of one family, the hypercharge coefficient is 2⁢(−(−1)3+6⁢(16)3−3⁢(23)3+2⁢(−12)3−3⁢(−13)3), which is zero; the mixed coefficients, −(12)+3⁢(16) for hypercharge with two W fields and 2⁢(16)−(−(13)+(23)) for hypercharge with two gluons, and the SU(3) coefficient, one half of (2 − 1 − 1), vanish as well (in units of the couplings). Hence the parity-odd part of X1 vanishes, the parity-odd monomials get zero coefficients and ΔSST(1) contains no Levi-Civita symbol. The report confirms numerically that the parity-odd parts of the single multiplets, of order 102, cancel to below 10−13. The automation detects an anomalous content and stops with an error.

broken-shift.title: The broken phase as a change of variable
broken-shift.body:
The broken phase is not renormalised anew. Its action is the renormalised action of the unbroken phase, Sren=S0+δS(1)+ΔSST(1), written in the variable φ=H−Hv: the Higgs doublet is shifted, H→Hv+φ, by the constant doublet Hv whose upper component vanishes and whose lower component is v2, in the same linear gauge and at ξ=1. No loop calculation beyond those of the unbroken phase enters.

The report gives three reasons why this is exact. The shift is a change of variable: Hv is constant, so derivatives and functional derivatives with respect to H and φ coincide, and the effective action of the broken phase is that of the unbroken phase at Hv+φ, with tadpole graphs part of every Green's function. The counterterms are local polynomials in H: the poles and the finite breaking X1 are fixed by their Taylor coefficients at H=0, and the Taylor operator counts every mass and every vertex proportional to v as a small quantity, so the coefficients computed with massless propagators are the complete one-loop input. The gauge fixing does not depend on H: the Slavnov–Taylor operator and the linear identities keep their form, the breaking Δ1 does not involve H, and the BRST transformation of the fluctuation is 𝐬φ=i⁢𝛚(Hv+φ). Rigid SU(2)×U(1) invariance stays exact, realised non-linearly on φ.

The vacuum value v is not a parameter of the action: it is defined by the minimum of the tree-level potential written with the MS-bar parameters, m2=−λ⁢v2 with m2 negative (tadpoles). No input from an Rξ gauge is used. That gauge depends on Hv and is a different action: it breaks rigid invariance unless Hv is replaced by an external doublet, and it needs Green's functions that the report lists but does not compute (Section 5.5.3).

broken-masses.title: Masses and mass counterterms in the broken phase
broken-masses.body:
The tree-level masses are MW=g⁢v2, MZ=MWcW with cW=gg2+g′2, Mh2=2⁢λ⁢v2 and mk=yk⁢v2 for k = u, d, e; the photon, the gluons, the neutrino, the Goldstone fields G0, G+ and all ghosts are massless in this gauge. They are MS-bar masses at the tree-level minimum, not pole masses. The massive Dirac fields are built from physical components, for example u=PRU+PLΨQ1, and their sterile partners from the χf, u′=PLU+PRΨQ1, where ΨQ1 is the upper SU(2) component of the quark doublet.

The sterile partners change the fermion propagator. The mass term couples only the physical components, while the d-dimensional kinetic term couples u and u′ through /pˆ. The propagator of the pair has the denominator (p2)2−mu2⁢p‾2, which is not d-dimensionally covariant; its physical block reduces to the standard i⁢(mu+/p‾)p‾2−mu2 at vanishing hatted momentum, where external fermions live. The R-operation is unchanged: the mass can be treated as a two-point insertion on massless propagators, so poles and the finite breaking are polynomials in the masses. At one loop the finite parts can be traded for those of the standard propagator plus a local term (Section 5.5.2); beyond one loop this is not derived.

The mass counterterms follow from the unbroken-phase constants by the shift. In units of 116π21ϵ, δMW2MW2 is −Y˜−133g2+12g′2, with Y˜=3⁢yu2+3⁢yd2+ye2; the bare-mass shift of the up quark, δmu=mu⁢(δZH2+δyuyu), is mu⁢(−38g2−1124g′2+34(yu2−yd2)−4⁢gs2); and δMh2=Mh2⁢(δZH+δλλ). Under the normalisation (N1) there is no finite counterterm for the fermion masses, the Yukawa vertices or the scalar potential; the gauge bosons receive finite mass-like terms (finite terms after the shift). Not computed: broken-phase finite parts at non-zero external momenta.

broken-mixing.title: Gauge–Goldstone and neutral gauge mixing
broken-mixing.body:
The neutral gauge fields are rotated with the weak mixing angle, Zμ=cW⁢Wμ3−sW⁢Bμ and Aμγ=cW⁢Bμ+sW⁢Wμ3, with e=g⁢sW; the same rotation is applied to the ghosts, antighosts, auxiliary fields and sources. Because the gauge fixing is linear and does not depend on H, the tree-level mixing between gauge and Goldstone fields stays in the quadratic action,

MW⁢i⁢(−Wμ+∂μG−+Wμ−∂μG+)+MZ⁢Zμ∂μG0

and enters the propagators: there are mixed gauge–Goldstone propagators and double poles at k2=0 in the longitudinal and Goldstone parts. This is a consistent gauge, in which the broken-phase action is complete. The Rξ gauge would cancel this mixing but is a different action (the shift).

The singular counterterm mixes the neutral fields. The field constants of Zμ and Aμγ form a matrix, the rotation of the diagonal matrix of δZW and δZB; in units of 116π21ϵ its entries are 118(33⁢g2⁢cW2−43⁢g′2⁢sW2) for Z Z, −59e2 for the photon and 118cW⁢sW⁢(33⁢g2+43⁢g′2) for the Z–photon element. In the same units the mass counterterm contains the Z–photon term −2⁢g2⁢cW⁢sW⁢MZ2⁢ZμAγμ and no photon mass term, and the mixing counterterm contains a new term −2⁢g2⁢cW⁢sW⁢MZ⁢Aμγ∂μG0. The Yukawa parts of these counterterms multiply barred components only, since they come from fermion loops.

The finite restoring counterterm changes the mixing by −13Y˜ times the tree-level mixing above (times 116π2), with Y˜=3⁢yu2+3⁢yd2+ye2; it comes from the current monomials of the unbroken phase. There is no finite photon–Goldstone term, because the two current coefficients are equal, and no finite gauge–Higgs term. The longitudinal and mixing terms change only unphysical parts of the two-point functions, but they enter every loop calculation in this gauge.

broken-tadpole.title: Tadpoles and the vacuum value
broken-tadpole.body:
The vacuum value v is defined by the minimum of the tree-level potential written with the MS-bar renormalised parameters, m2=−λ⁢v2 with m2 negative. It is a function of m2 and λ, not a parameter of the action, and it is not renormalised. With this convention the tree-level tadpole term −v⁢h⁢(λ⁢v2+m2) vanishes, while the tadpole graphs are kept in every Green's function; this is the treatment of Fleischer and Jegerlehner.

The singular counterterm then contains a tadpole term −v⁢h⁢δT with

δT=λ⁢v2⁢δZH+δm2+v2⁢δλ

which equals 116π21ϵ⁢v2⁢(−λ⁢CH+316⁢G4−Y4+6⁢λ2), with CH=3⁢g24+g′24, Y4=3⁢yu4+3⁢yd4+ye4 and G4=2⁢g2⁢g′2+3⁢g4+g′4. It cancels the pole of the one-loop tadpole; it contains the field-renormalisation part λ⁢v2⁢δZH besides δm2+v2⁢δλ. The Goldstone mass counterterm equals δT, as required by the relation between the Goldstone two-point function at zero momentum and the tadpole. Only the λ2 part of the tadpole pole was checked by hand; the finite part of the one-loop tadpole is not computed in the report. The finite restoring counterterm gives no tadpole and no scalar two-point term.

Other conventions differ by a finite reparametrisation of v. If the renormalised tadpole is set to zero, v is the minimum of the effective potential, which depends on the gauge, and the MS-bar masses depend on ξ. With a non-anticommuting γ5 the gauge independence of the convention used here is expected to need the restored identity and a control of the ξ dependence; this is not derived, and the report works at ξ=1 only.

broken-st.title: Finite restoring counterterms after the shift
broken-st.body:
The finite counterterm of the broken phase is ΔSST(1) evaluated at H=Hv+φ; no coefficient is recomputed. Its H-dependent coefficients are purely Yukawa, so after the shift the terms with Hv are proportional to fermion masses squared. They give the gauge bosons finite mass-like terms (times 116π2):

−12gs2⁢(mu2+md2)⁢GμAGAμ−12g2⁢(3⁢mu2+3⁢md2+me2)⁢Wμ+W−μ−e2⁢(43mu2+13md2+me2)⁢AμγAγμ

and Z–Z and Z–photon terms. For two neutral bosons the term has the form of a mass term, one half of 116π2 times the two fields times −2⁢∑fmf2⁢(3⁢af′⁢af+vf′⁢vf)⁢Nfc, with vf, af the vector and axial couplings of the fermion f to the first boson, primed for the second, and Nfc its colour multiplicity. Under the shift the current terms change the gauge–Goldstone mixing by −13Y˜ times its tree value, and the h-linear terms are 2⁢hv times the mass-like ones.

The photon and gluon mass terms look alarming but are required. The report computes the fermion-loop two-point functions of the photon, of Z–photon and of the gluon at zero momentum, to order mf2, with complete finite parts. The finite local part per fermion is 263⁢af′⁢af+2⁢vf′⁢vf; of it, 143⁢af′⁢af−2⁢vf′⁢vf comes from the difference between the propagator with sterile partners and the standard one. The counterterm contributes −2⁢(3⁢af′⁢af+vf′⁢vf), and the sum, 83⁢af′⁢af, vanishes for the photon, Z–photon and gluon cases, where one of the couplings is vectorial. The photon, Z–photon and gluon two-point functions at zero momentum therefore stay massless; an independent evaluation through the Slavnov–Taylor identity of the ghost–photon legs gives the same constant (Section 5.4.6).

The longitudinal terms, for example 23g2⁢(∂μW+μ)∂νW−ν and 89e2⁢(∂μAγμ)2, and the mixing change only unphysical parts. The W and Z poles depend on the mass-like coefficients and therefore on the restoring counterterm. The remaining 33 non-zero coefficients multiply monomials without H and are untouched by the shift.

broken-interactions.title: Interaction terms generated by the shift
broken-interactions.body:
Every interaction of the broken phase descends from an operator of the unbroken phase under H→Hv+φ, with φ containing the Higgs boson h and the Goldstone fields G0, G+, G−. The scalar kinetic term gives the couplings of h to W+W− and ZZ, for instance 2⁢h⁢(12MZ2⁢ZμZμ+MW2⁢Wμ+W−μ)v, and Goldstone–gauge–gauge vertices; the potential gives cubic and quartic scalar couplings proportional to λ⁢v and λ; the Yukawa terms give −mf⁢(1+hv)⁢f‾f together with G0 couplings with γ5 and G+ couplings with chiral projectors, all with physical components only. In the fermion currents the charged fields couple with g2 times the raising and lowering combinations of Pauli matrices, the photon with e⁢q and the Z with g⁢(T3−sW2⁢q)cW, where q is the charge matrix and T3 the third isospin generator. Ghosts couple only to gauge fields, so there is no ghost–scalar vertex in this gauge; the Higgs source term gives a source–ghost two-point vertex proportional to MW and MZ.

The singular counterterms of these vertices are those of the unbroken phase at Hv+φ. The quartic scalar coupling carries 2⁢λ⁢δZH+δλ, equal to 116π21ϵ⁢(−2⁢λ⁢CH+316⁢G4−Y4+12⁢λ2), and so do the cubic couplings proportional to v; every Yukawa-derived term of fermion k, mass term included, carries the factor ck of the Yukawa vertex; the fermion currents carry −116π21ϵ⁢(Cf+Cad(r)+𝒴f) for the factor r; the cubic and quartic gauge self-couplings keep their unbroken-phase factors.

The finite restoring counterterm adds, besides the mass-like terms, the h-linear and h2 terms (2⁢hv and h2v2 times the mass-like ones), −13Y˜ times the tree scalar–scalar–gauge vertices, the vertex −MW⁢(yu2+2⁢yd2)⁢(−g′⁢sW⁢Zμ+e⁢Aμγ)(G+W−μ+G−W+μ), further scalar–scalar–gauge–gauge terms, and the fermion–gauge vertices and source terms of the unbroken phase rewritten in the mass basis. In each Exposé of the broken phase the graphs shown are those of the parent operators of the unbroken phase.
